items.title: Achilles can never catch the tortoise
items.claim: Zeno's paradox: Achilles gives the tortoise a head start. To catch it, he must reach where the tortoise was — by then the tortoise has moved a bit. Repeat infinitely. He performs infinitely many tasks and can never reach the tortoise.

options.text: Achilles is actually slower than the tortoise
Infinitely many finite tasks can take finite total time — the geometric series 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... sums to 1, not infinity

items.reveal_title: Zeno's paradoxes and the calculus that resolves them
items.reveal:
Zeno of Elea (c. 490-430 BC) offered several paradoxes about motion:
- Dichotomy: to walk across a room, you must first walk half-way, then half of what remains, etc. Infinite steps.
- Achilles and the tortoise: as above.
- Arrow: at each instant, an arrow occupies a fixed position, so it isn't moving — yet motion sums to a journey.

Resolution requires the concept of convergent infinite series — formalised in the 17th and 19th centuries by Newton, Leibniz, Cauchy and Weierstrass. The sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... equals 2, not infinity. Infinitely many tasks can be completed in finite time, provided their durations form a convergent series.

The paradoxes pre-dated rigorous calculus by 2000 years. Zeno's challenge actually pushed mathematicians toward developing the tools needed to handle infinity and the continuum properly. Mathematicians sometimes joke that Zeno was the first calculus student to fail to grasp limits.
items.why: Common sense rules out infinite tasks in finite time. Mathematical analysis shows infinite tasks of decreasing size can totalise to finite quantities — and motion proceeds.

items.title: 1 is the first digit of natural numbers 30% of the time
items.claim: Take any 'natural' set of numbers — house prices, river lengths, populations, physical constants. Look at the first digit. About 30% start with 1. Only 4.6% start with 9. The pattern is so reliable that auditors use it to detect fraud.

options.text: Benford's law: for scale-invariant distributions, the probability of first digit d is log10(1 + 1/d). The math reflects that doubling a number (or scaling by any factor) takes longer to pass through 1-2 than through 8-9 on a logarithmic axis

items.reveal:
Simon Newcomb (1881) noticed that the early pages of his logarithm tables (corresponding to leading digit 1) were more worn than the later pages. He inferred something about how often various leading digits appeared.

Frank Benford (1938, physicist) systematically tested the rule across many datasets (river lengths, populations, atomic weights, baseball stats, addresses). He found:
Digit 1: 30.1%
Digit 2: 17.6%
Digit 3: 12.5%
Digit 4: 9.7%
Digit 5: 7.9%
Digit 6: 6.7%
Digit 7: 5.8%
Digit 8: 5.1%
Digit 9: 4.6%
Formula: P(d) = log10(1 + 1/d).

Why: many natural quantities span multiple orders of magnitude. On a logarithmic scale, the spacing from 1 to 2 (log 2 ≈ 0.30) is much wider than from 9 to 10 (log 10/9 ≈ 0.046). If the distribution is roughly uniform in log space, leading digits follow Benford.

Applications:
- Forensic accounting: real financial data follow Benford; fabricated numbers usually don't. Auditors flag tax returns or financial statements that deviate.
- Election fraud detection: ballot counts in honest elections follow Benford; many disputed elections have shown deviations.
- Scientific fraud detection: many cases of data fabrication caught.
- Image authenticity: pixel JPEG coefficients follow Benford-like distributions; fakes often don't.

Limitations: Benford requires scale-invariant data spanning multiple orders of magnitude. Constrained data (height, ages) don't satisfy it. Carefully fabricated data designed to fool Benford also exist.

The mathematical generalisation: any distribution with logarithmic density invariant under scaling will produce Benford's law for leading digits.
items.why: Random-looking data often follow precise patterns. Benford's law is counterintuitive and has practical applications in fraud detection. It's also a window into how scale-invariance shapes the structure of numbers we encounter.

items.title: Compounding interest infinitely fast gives the same answer as compounding once
items.claim: Invest 1 dollar at 100 percent annual interest. Compounded once a year: 2 dollars. Twice: 2.25. Monthly: 2.61. Continuously: 2.71828... — the constant e. Not infinity, not 2 — a specific irrational number.
items.prompt: Why does compounding infinitely often give a finite limit?

options.text: (1 + 1/n) to the power n is bounded above by 3 for all n, and increases monotonically; its limit as n approaches infinity is e, a fundamental constant of growth
Each compounding adds tiny amounts that cancel each other
Math caps results at e by definition

items.reveal:
Jacob Bernoulli, investigating compound interest, asked what happens as compounding frequency goes to infinity. He calculated (1 + 1/n) to the power n for ever-larger n and found the values approached a specific number between 2.71 and 2.72.

The number is e — base of the natural logarithm. It shows up everywhere: continuous growth (e to the rt), the normal distribution (Gauss), Euler's identity (e to the i pi equals minus 1), derangements in combinatorics, and the most-common-digit problem (Benford's law).

e can be characterised many ways:
- Limit of (1 + 1/n) to the power n.
- Infinite sum 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + 1/3! + ...
- Unique number whose exponential function equals its own derivative.

Like pi, e is transcendental — no polynomial with rational coefficients has e as a root.
items.why: Compounding 'more often' sounds like it should produce ever-larger returns. The limit is finite because each compounding period adds proportionally less.
